autun.c: AUTUN (Bibracte, Augustodunum), a town in France, department of the Si ire, in the Burgunaian district of Autiuiois. Pop. 9348. It is situated on the river Arroux, is the seat of a bishop, and has a fine cathedral. Cloth, carpets, leather, stockings, and paper are manufactured in the i ■lace. — The ancient Bibracte was the clii i of the JEdiii, and had a much frequented Druid school; and at a later period, under the Romans, when ' "lunnm, it was no less famous for its school of rhetoric. A. was d by the Saracens in 725, and nearly destroyed by the Normans in SS8. There still exist at A. many ruins of Roman temples, gates, triumphal arches, and other antiquities. At the Council of A. (109-1), King Philip T. was excommunicated for divorcing his ", Bertha.

auvergne.c: AUVERGNE, a southern central district of France, was before the revolution a separate province , composing almost exclusively the i departments of Cantal and Puy-de-Dome. Between the Allier and the upper course of the Dordogno and the Lot, A. rises into a highland region, having Bourbonnais, Limousin, and Kouergue, as terraces cent int. i the western plains, while on t it joins the Cevennes and the southern hi- Not only do the cone and dome-like shapes of tho 678 summits betray a volcanic formation, but also tho great masses of basalt and trachyte that break through the crust of gra ite as I ider it le that this was a chief focus of plu action. Among tho summits that have apparently been at one time volcanoi , the mo b remarkable are Cantal (G093), Mont-d'Or (6188), Puy-de I (4S0G), and Parion ; the latter, adjoining Puy-de- DAme, is basin-shaped on the top, and one of the finest specimens of an ancient and extinct volcano i all are now covered with verdure, A. falls naturally into two divisions — Upper A., to the south, and Lower A., to the north ; in which last the valley of Limagne. on the left bank of the Allier, is distinguished for extraordinary fertility. The dim colder in the mountainous districts than the southern position, with a less elevation, would lead OS to expect, and is remarkable for furious winds and violent thunder-storms ; but in the deep valleys tho heat of summer is often oppressive. The lava- covered plateaus are desert, but the puh volcanic earths that cover the slopes and valleys form a rich and fruitful soil, as is shewn by the crops of grain, garden produce, fine fruits, wine, abundance of chestnuts in the south, and of walnuts in the north, as well as by extensive thriving fon ta, .. ith flax and hemp fields and meadow-lauds, poorer districts. Agriculture is in a rather neglected condition ; but the breeding of cattle, Hy of mules, is well managed. A. produces iron, lead, copper, antimony, ami coal, and is rich in mineral springs. The Auvergnese are a highland people, ru manners, poor, ignorant, at the same time honest and kind, though not free from the propensity to revenge. They live by cattle-keeping and agriculture, and by going to Paris as labo Domestic manufactures, therefore, remain confine 1 to weaving, tanning, and paper-making. A. has, however, produced distinguished men. It was tho native place of statesmen aud warriors of the 15th and 10th centuries; aud also of the Arnauld (q. v.) family, so distinguished in tho history of Port Royal and of Jansenism. In moro recent times, tte and Polignac may be named. Cliief towns, Clermont and Aurillac (q. v.). The country derived its name from the Averni, who Ion I tin ir fastnesses against Ca;sar, as later against the Goths, Burgundians, and Franks, with whom they at last coalesced.

auxerre.c:
AUXERRE (anc. Auttssiodorutv), chief town of the dop. of Yoime, France, stands on the Yonne, 90 miles south-east from Paris, with which it is connected by railway. It is situated on the slope of a hill, in a rich and beautiful district abounding in vineyards ; but the city itself is generally ill built, the streets narrow, crooked, and dirt}'. Its aspect from a distance is very imposing, the most i>romiucnt feature being the cathedral, a gi'aiul aud beautiful cdilicc. It is dedicated to St Stephen, aud although part of it is as old as the I3th c., it is not yet completed. The gTcater p.oil of it is in the Flamboyant style, but the choir is in the Early Gothic. The pauitcd glass of the windows is very splendiiL The chapter of A. was at one time one of the richest in France. The church of St Germain is another line building, with a lofty choir and transepts, and a very ancient detached tower. It contains crypts in which are the tombs of the early counts of Auxerre. The cluirch of St Pierre is a beautiful specimen of the Italianised Gothic, built in the 16th and 17th centuries. There is a curious old clock-tower over a gate-house, with an ugly skeleton spire of iron bars. The ancient walls of the city have been converted into boulevards. A. was a flourishing town before the Roman invasion of Gaid. It successfully resisted the Huns under Attila, who only ravaged its suburbs. Clovis took it from the Romans. After his death, it became part of the kingdom of Burgundy. 1'he English took it iu 1359, but it was retaken by Du Guescliu. Charles VII. gave it up to the Duke of Burgimdy. It was finally imited to the kingdom of France by 411

I.oiiis XI. It 11.15 a coinnuinal collcu'c, a imiscum of aiitiiniitios, and a liotanio Kanleii. The princijial niamifaotuiTS are of strings fur musical instruments, woollen cloths, hosiery, "earthenware, ami leather. The Yonne becomes navigable here, ami large quintities of Burgundy wines are sent down it to I'ai-is ; there is also a considei-able ex|port trade in timber and in charcoal. Pop. (1SG6) l;i,0G2.

ava.c: AVA, a mined city of Burmah, of which it has dly b. en the capital, the honour having been transferred again and again between it and Mon- chobo, Sagaing, and Amarapura, which is the present capital. It stands in kit 21° 51' N., long. 95° 5S' E., on the south-east bank of the Irawnddy, here about 4000 feet broad. The river at this point receives two allluents, and these being joined by a canal, the city is rendered circnmnavigable. The name is a Hindu and Malay corruption of Ai or Aaen-ua, meaning JUsk-pond, given it from I built where there were formerly lish-ponds, of which some still remain; but in official documents it is ■ ited as Ratnapura, i.e., City of Pearls. The city, which is, or was, eight or ten miles in circmn- . is surrounded by walls and ditches. A. is now almost a desert, having been reduced to ruins by an earthquake in 1S39. — On the opposite bank stands the city of Sagaing, which has twice been the seat of government. The united populi tion of the three cities of Ava, Sagaing, and Amarajmra, t one time estimated at 4U0,0U0.

A'VA, ARVA, YAVA, or KAYA (Macropiper methyslicum), a plant of the natural order Piperacece (q .v.), possessing narcotic properties. Until recently, it was ranked in the genus Piper (Pepper). It is a shrubby plant, with heart-shaped, aciiiuinate ' and very short, solitary, axillary spikes of Be It ifl a native of many of the South-sea islands, ih" inhabitants intoxicate themselves with a fermented liquor prepared from its root or (more accurately) rhizome. The rhizome is thick, woody, n 1, and aromatic. A tincture of it is useful in chronic rheumatisms. The intoxicating liquor is ed by macerating it in water. The Taliitians were accustomed to prepare it in a very manner; much as the Indians of the Andes ■ CIrica or Maize beer — chewing the root, ting it in a bowl, straining through cocoa-nut and mixing with water or cocoa-nut milk, after which fermentation speedily ensues. The taste is unpleasant to those unaccustomed to it, and has been ; ed to that of rhubarb and magnesia. Tin; intoxication is not like that produced by I spirits, but rather a stupefaction like that caused by opium. It is succeeded by a copious perspiration . The habitual use of ava causes a whitish sciu-f on the skin, which, among the heathen Tahitians, was reckoned a badge of nobility, the common people not having the means of indulgence requisite to produce it. — The leaf of tl plant is in some places used with the betel-nut, instead of that of the betel-pepper.

avalajfches.c: A'VALAJf CHES are masses of snow or ice that slide or roll down the declivities of high mountain •, and often occasion great devastation. They have various names, according to their nature. Drift or powder avalanches (Staul> Lavinen) consist of snow, which, loose and dry from strong frost, once set in motion by the wind, accumulates in its descent, and comes suddenly into the valley in an overwhelming dust-cloud. A. of this kind occur chiefly in winter, and are dangerous on account of their suddenness, suffocating men and animals, and overturning houses by the compression of the air which they cause. Another kind of avalanche resembles a landslip . When the snow begins to melt in spring, the soil beneath becomes loose and slippery ; and the snow slides down the declivity by its own weight, carrying with it soil, trees, and rocks. The greatest danger is where elevated tracts of moderate declivity are separated from the valleys by precipitous walls of rock; the softened snow of spring beginning to roll or slide on these slopes, is hurled over the precipices with fearful force into the valleys. The very wind caused prostrates forests and houses. Ice A. are those that are seen and heard in summer thundering down the steeps, e. g., of the Jungf rau. They consist of masses of ice that detach them from the glaciers in the upper regions. They are most common in July, August, and September.

avallox.c: AVALLOX (anc. Ahallo), a town of the dep. of Yonae, France, 26 miles south-e.-ist from Auxcrre, on a steep liill of red granite, nearly surrounded by the Cousin, wliieli here Hows through a ravine. Around the town runs a broad terrace- wall, shaded with lime-trees, about 50'.) feet above the bed of the river. The surrounding country is fertile, yielding much wine and grain, and abounding also in excellent pastures, on which great numljcrs of cattle and sheep are fed. The town is generally well built, and has broad and clean streets. The church is ancient, and has a curious Romauesquo portal. If any number of unequal quanti- ■ given, another quantity may be found of a or intermediate magnitude, some of the given quantities being greater, and others less, than the one found, which is called the average. The exact relation is this : that the sum of the excesses of the greater above the A. is equal to the sum of the i of the less below it. If there are, say, 7 unequally tilled with sand, and if we take handfuls from the greater, and add these to the less, until the sand is equally distributed, then any one : of the equalised measures of sand is the A. of the I 7 unequal measures. If the quantities of sand in

Ihe sum being 63, this, divided by 7, gives !i ounces as the average. The system of averaging is a very important and time-saving one. If a farmer, for instance, has three lots of cattle, the first of which he averages at £25 a head, the second at £15, and the third at £9, it might be thought tha the whole stock made up of the three lots would be got by taking the mean of £25, £15, and £9— viz., 25 + 15-j-ri ' . But this would be correct only if there were an equal numli.T mi cattle in each of the lots. To gel I e real A in case of the lots being unequal, he must multiply the A. of each lot by the number of cattle in it, add the three products b igether, and divide 1 ly the whole number of cattle in all three lots taken together. A rule was established by the Bhodian law (q. v.), and has prevailed in every maritime nation, that where a loss has been sustained, or expense incurred, for the general safety of the ship and cargo, a contribution should be made, in proportion to their respective interests, by the owners of the ship, freight, and goods on board ; or, in modern times, by the insurers of these. To this contribution the name of 6 A. is given. The apparel, jewels, and other personal property of the passengers, not carried for purposes of traffic, and the seamen's wages and provisions, are net liable for any share in this contribution. Good; thrown overboard are now estimated at the price they would have yielded at the port of delivery at the time, freight, duties, &C., being deducted. See JETTISON. Pa .1., again, is the loss of an anchor, the starting of a plank, the leaking of a cask, the goods washed from the deck, or the like, where the common safety was not in question, and where there is. consequently, no contribution. To losses of this description, the term A., though generally, is incorrectly applied. Petty Averages are the di anchorage, pilotage, Ac. If these occur in the ordinary course of the voyage, they are not loss, but i in; ly part of the expense necessarily in But if they have been incurred in extraordinary circumstances, and for the purpose of avoiding impending danger, they are a loss which is included in the general A., and covered by the contribution. A. Bond is a deed which parties liable to a A. are in the habit of executing, by which they rwer an arbiter to value the property lost, and fix the proportion which shall be borne by each proprietor.

AVERRHO'ES, properly, Ibn Roshd, or more full}', Abul-Walid Mohann. | Ahmcd-lhn, Mohammed-Ibn-Boshd, the most famous of the Arabian philosophers, was born at Cordova, in Spain, in 1149. His father, who was chief judge and mufti, instructed him in Mohammedan jurisprudence . In theology and philosophy, he had fhophail for his teacher; and in medicine, Ibn Zohr, the elder. His talents ami acquirements made him be appointed sue© father, and afterwards chief judge in the province of Mauritania. Being accused, out of envy, of a departure from the orthodox doctrines of Mohammedanism, he was in his office, and condemned by the ecclesiastical tribunal of Maroceo to recant his heretical opinions, and do penance. After this, he returned to his native place, and lived in great poverty, until the Calif Almansor reinstated him in hi- 0 which he went back to Maroceo, where he died in 1198 or 1206. A. regarded Aristotle as the gi of all philosophers. He translated and illustrated Aristotle's writings with great penetration; but the influence of the Alexandrine view laid down in the commentaries of Ammonius, Themistius. and others, is easily seen in his works, as in those of most of the Arabian philosophers. In opposition to the Arabian orthodox school, especially against Algazali, A. forth on the side of reason as the defender of philosophy . The Arabians called him, by way of eminence, the Expositor (of Aristotle), and his Syriac translation of Aristotle was held in the highest esteem among them. His writings are known to us only through Latin translations (Yen. 1489). His I mi atari a on Aristotle appeared in an edition of that philosopher's works ill vols. Ven. 1560). He rote a sort of medical iiich, under the name of ' corruption of the Arab :. e., 'The To! I' system), * b into Latin, and repeatedly printed (Ven. 1482 l."d4). The philosophy of A. attained to importance in the Christian Church as early as the 13th C, although his panthi istic doctrine of the unity of the active principle in the universe was often repudiated as an error, and astrology was characterised as Averrhoism. axiom.c: A'XIOM, a Greek word meaning a demand or . is commonly used to signify a general proposition, which the understanding recogm true, as soon as the import of the words conveying it is apprehended. Of this kind, for example, are all propositions whose predicate is a property essential to our notion of the subject. Every rational science requires such fundamental propositions , from which all the truths composing it are derived ; the whole of geometry, for instance, rests on, comparatively, a very few axioms. Whether there is. for the whole of human know any single, absolutely first A., from which all else that is known may be deduced, is a question that has given rise to much disputation ; but the fact, that human knowledge may have various starting- points, answers it in the negative. Mathematicians word A. to denote those propositions which they must assume as known from some other source than deductive reasoning, and employ in proving all the other truths of the science. The di axioms and postulates is usually stated in this way : an A. is -a theorem granted without demonstra a postulate is 'a problem granted without constructions — as, To draw a straight line between two given points.

At an early date. A. was a commercial and military place of some importance. William the Lion made it a royal burgh about 1202. During the Scottish wars of independence, it formed a regular centre of military operations, and, while in possession of an rrison, it was the scene ... AYUNTAMIE'NTO is the name given in Spain to the councils or governing bodies of towns. Sprung istitutions of the Romans, and firmly established during the long struggles w ith the Moors, the ayuntamientos acquired great influenc political power, the more eo that the nobility were not excluded from them. Although this impjm d through the insurrection of Juan de Padilla in 1521; and at a later period, under the Bourbons, the last shadow of municipal freedom was lost ; the remembrance of it continn rished by the i pie. \ cordingly, the corb a of Cadis, in lSl'J, took up the leading features of the former i. adapting them, by more democratic modifications , to the requirements of the time. On burn of Ferdinand VTL, the ayuntami were abolished ; they were again restored by the 0*3

cortes, in 1823; and after the invasion by I once more set aside. Daring the civil proposals were maden the ayuntanu d1 a ol 1812 were ooi by the constitution of 1S37. According I statute, the A., with the alcalde as presid appointr. 1 by the Eree choice of tho people, ami is entitled to exercise the motions within the circle of its jurisdiction. ionally annul its acts, but must afterwards procure the ratification of the cortes, by which alone an A. can be dissolved. The ayontamientos are empowered to make op the lists of electors and jurors, to organise the national guards, to command olios within tlnir own bounds, to direct the apportionment and raisin',' of taxes, and to manage the funds of the commune. In 1S40, a bi] brought into the cortes, formed on the model of French law, proposing to deprive the aj mientos of all political power, and r functions to purely municipal matters, and also to limit the franchise to the most highly taxed. But isurrection which this step excited, and which ended in the expulsion of the queen, Marii I prevented the imijcct from being carried out, At last, in 1844, a law, similar to that proposed in 1S40, was, through the intriguing of Christina, supp by French influence, adopted by the cortes, then composed of moderados ; and this law, with little alteration, continues in force to the present day.

Both have nearly white flowers, very beautiful, and Of delirious fragrance. A. I 1 with glutinous hairs like A. Pontica; but I iwere of A. nudiflora are nearly death them. Both species abound from Canada to the southern parts of the United States. They are taller shrubs than A. Pontica. Upon account of its sweet smell, A. nudiflora is called in A the Upright Honeysuckle. A. », a native of the southern parts of the United States, ribed as frequently clothing the mountains with a robe of living scarlet. — India and China produce several species of A., of which one of the finest is A. azeglio.c:
AZE'GLIO, Ma'ssdio Marquis d', famous as an artist, a publicist, a romance-writer, and a I man, is the descendant of an ancient and noble family of Piedmont. He was born in 1801 at Turin, bis father held a high military position. In his fifteenth year, A. followed his father to Borne, where he had been appointed ambassador, and there contracted a love for the fine arts ; but his study of music and painting was cut short by his father procuring him an appointment in a Piedmontese cavalry nt. Hero A. devoted his leisure with such intensity to scientific pursuits, that he brought on an illness which forced, him to quit the service. A journey to Piome, from which he returned to Turin in 1 21 1, restored his health, but deepened his passii hi fi .r painting. After some difficulty, he got his 1 permission to devote himself entirely to this art. A year had hardly elapsed ere A. had made himself a name in Rome as an artist. In landscape-painting he soon attained complete artistic skill. After a residence of eight years at Home, during which he had pursued the study of history along with painting, he returned to Turin. On the death of his father in 1830, he went to Milan, where, painting was then flourishing. In Milan he made the friendship of Alexander Manzoui, whose daughter ho married. A. now began to make himself favourably known also in literature, his novels, Ellore J mosco (1833), and Niccolo di Lean (1841), having done much to fan the national spirit of the Italians. The political affairs of Italy soon occupied him ively; he traversed the provinces, cities, and villages, seeking to stir up the spirit of patriotism, and to conciliate the unhappy party divisions, and

wa3 everywhere received with rejoicing and acclamation . A. never belonged to a secret political society, ljut opposed conspiracies as mischievous, and exhorted the impatient to moderation. While in Florence, he wrote his famous piece, Deijli Casi di Romagna, in which he lashed the miserable j papal government, denounced the vain attempts at insurrection, and proved to the Italian princes the necessity of a national policy. After the election of Pius IX. as pope, A. returned to Home, ami ti> his influence were ascribed the reforms with which Pius began his government. He was intensely active at this time, and wrote much on public questions. (The whole of his political writ- coDected in one volume, appeared at Turin. 1851.) When Charles Albert, after the rising of !.ly, crossed the Ticino, A. left Eome with the papal I ined to support the Italian contest. In the battle of Vicenza, where he commanded a legion, he was severely wounded in the leg while fighting at the 'head of his troops. ly was he recovered, when with his pen he courageously opposed the republican party, now intoxicated with victory. On the opening of the Sardinian parliament, he was chosen a member of the Chamber of Deputies. After the unfortunate event of the battle of Koran, the young king, Victor Emanuel II., appointed him (1849) president of the cabinet, an office which he undertook solely out of love to his king and country. His influence in this high position was most beneficial, Sardinia owing much of the prosperity and proud national position she now enjoys to his foo and sagacity. At the close of the late war (1859), when several important towns in the States of the Church declared for Piedmont, A. was appointed (pro tempore) General and Commissioner Extraordinary , purely military, for the Roman States. On hi3 retirement, he issued a proclamation to the people, which greatly tended to strengthen their resolution by its noble yet temperate advice.

azerbijan.c: AZERBIJA'N, or ADEKBAIJA'X, the ancient Media Atropatene, is the most northerly province of Persia. It is situated between 1st 30' ami 4 long. 44° and 48' 40' E. ; bounded on the S. by i Kurdistan and Irak, E by Ghilan, X.E. ami N. by the Russian territory, and W. by Turkish Kurdistan. It has an area of about 30,(K)0 square miles, and a population of 2,000,000. The surface of A. is very mountainous, many of the ranges rising from 7000 to 9000 feet in height The peak of Savalan (an extinct volcano) reaches an elevation of 13,000 feet. Mount Ararat rises on the north-west border. The chief rivers of A. are the Aras or Arcuce.% the Kara Su. and the Khdl-Uzen. The salt lake Urumiyah or Urnmieyeh (q. v.), the largest in Persia, is situated on the western border of the province. The climate of A. is not unhealthy, but it is subject to the extremes of heat and cold. The transition from cold to heat is very rapid. In the mountainous districts, the hail-storms are occasionally so violent as to kill cattle. The principal products of A. are rice, barley, wheat, maize, flax, hemp, cotton, tobacco, honey, and saffron ; camels, horses, cattle, and sheep are also reared ; velvet, silks, stuff, carpets, woollens, and leather are the most important articles of manufacture , and a little is done in hardware. Lead, iron, copper, sulphur, saltpetre, and salt are found in the province. The capital of A. is Tabriz, with a population of about 30,000. It has suffered greatly from earthquakes. The other towns of note are Urumiyah, on the lake of that name ; Maragna, famous as the place where Nasir Eddin, the asu ted his observatory; Miana, Khoi, Sehnas, and ArdcbiL

azimghur.c: AZIMGHU'R, or AZIM "S FORT, a name primarily applied to a town in India, and thence extended to ita district. 1. The town is in lat 26° N., and long. 83' 14' E. From Calcutta it is 448 miles to the north-west ; from Benares, 81 to the north ; from Allahabad, 109 to the north-east; and from Lucknow, 171 to the south-east. It is situated on the north-eastern Tons, a considerable offset of the Gogra, which is here crossed by a bridge of boats, and wluch is navigable downwards, a distance of 40 miles, to its confluence with the Surjoo. The town is estimated to contain about 14,11(10 inhabitants, besides the troops in garrison. During the mutiny of 1^-57, A. was, so far, a creditable exception to the general rule of ruthless cruelty among the insurgents. The sepoys did indeed mutiny, actuated , apparently, by a wish to appropriate a passing treasure of 7 lacs of rupees, or £70,000 si Rut, having formed a square round their officers, and sworn to protect them, they brought carriages for them and their families, and escorted the whole ten miles towards Ghazeepore. — 2. The district stretches in N. lat. between 25' 30' and 26 - and in E. long, between 82° 45' and S4 12'. Its area is said to be 2520 square miles ; and its population to be 1,313,950. These two estimates can scarcely be both correct, yielding, as they do, an average of 521 inhabitants to a square mile — a very ■ able average, more particularly as populous towns are unknown. The district is low and remarkably level. The sod is fertile, excepting that a few tracts are irreclaimably barren from being impregnated with soda, nitre, and other saline substances. There are tolerably extensive manufactures — the silk looms being 3122, and the cotton ones, 10,500. Connected with the latter is the curious fact, that scarcely any cotton-wool is produced on the spot

azimuth.c: AZIMUTH. The A. of a heavenly body is the angle measured along the horizon between the north or south point, and the point where a circle, passing through the zenith ami the body, cuts the horizon. The word comes from the Arabic, and is said to be derived from a word signifying a quarter of the heavens. It is usual to measure the A. westward from the point most remote from the el pole, beginning at 0°, and returning to it at 360". Thus, in northern Latitudes, where the north pole is 1. the A. is measured from the south point so that the east point, for instance, has an A. of 270'. See Apittt.t.a-bv Sphere. A. circles are those which extend from zenith to nadir, cutting the horizon at right angles, or those in which all the points have the same azimuth.

The principal members of the group are album a, present in white of eggs, and the juices of plants and animals ; globulim . or i rystalline, a variety of albumen found in the lens of the eye; vitelline, another variety of albumen, composing the ■ ii iter bulk of the yolk of the egg ; paralbumen, a third variety of albumen found in the animal system during certain diseases \fbrine, which occurs largely in the seeds of cereals and in animal muscle ; (or cheese matter), present in all milk; lego- mine, a variety of caseine found in pease, b and leguminous seeds in general: gelatine, which ent in the skin, bones, and other parts of animals; clumdrine, a variety of gelatine obtainable fr the cornea of the eye and the permanent cartilages ; isinglass, another variety of gelatine manufactured from the inner membrane of the bladder of sturgeons and other fishes; glue and Size, winch are secondary forms of gelatine; uric acid, and liippuric acid, which are present in the urine of the higher animals; kreatine and Icrealinine, occurring in the juice of flesh; several forms of urinary calculi, which are found as stones in the bladder; and the very large and important class of alkaloids, including strychnine, morphine, quinine, kc The principal members of the series of A. AZO'TUS, the Asfldod of the Old Testament (now Eedud), a village on the Mediterranean, -1 miles south of Jaffa. Lat. .'il1 45' N., long. .'Jt '■',"' E. It was formerly one of the chief citi the Philistines, strongly fortified, and the scene of numerous contests between that race and the Jews. Into this city the Ark of the < 'ovnant was brought by the Philistines, and placed m the temple of their god Dagon, whose image fell in pieces before it. In the 8th c. B.C., the town fell into the hands of the Assyrians ; and in the following century was

captured by the Egyptians, after a 20 years' blockade and siege. In the wars between Alexander Balas and Demetrius, A. was destroyed by lire. It was afterwards rebuilt by the Romans, but never regained its early importance. It has now a population of about 300, and the sea is gradually r. from its harbour.

azov.c: A'ZOV, or A'SO W, a fortress and port-town in the south of Russia, situated on the Don, about 20 miles from its mouth. The sand and mud deposited by the river have choked up the port, so that the trade and shipping of the place have dwindled away, and the 3000 inhabitants now depend mostly on fishing. A. was anciently a Greek colony, under the name of . and carried on extensive commerce with the in peoples. In number of inhabitants and in wealth it often rivalled Panticapaeum (now Kertch). In the 13th c. it was taken possession of by tin- Genoese, who called it Tana. They were driven out of it by Tinmr (Tamerlane) in 1392. In 1471, it was taken by the Turks, and since then has borne the name of A., the Turks calling the town and the iring sea Asak. After an obstinate sti-u^le, at which Peter the Great, then beginning his career, was present, it was captured by the Russians about the end of the 17th c. It more than once fell again under the dominion of the Turks, but at last, in 1771. remained in the undisturbed possession of Russia. It was bombarded and destroyed by an allied English and French squadron in ISoj.

aztecchildren.c: AZ'TEC CHILDREN. In the year 1S53, there were brought over to this country from America two diminutive children, a boy and a girl, said to be aged respectively 17 and 11, and who were represented as descendants of the ancient Aztecs. The height of each was under 3 feet, Their figure was slender and not ill-proportioned ; that which was chiefly remarkable being their features. While the id and chin receded, the nose was so singularly prominent as to suggest the idea of the face of a bird. Yet, with dark lively eyes, an olive complexion, and glossy long black hair, and a great fund of good-nature, they were far from unpli They spoke no intelligible language, but understood a few words of Fngbsh, and seemed to have a taste for music. Shewn to the public as curiosities, they were usually exhibited on a large table, on which they ran about amusing themselves. Their exhibitor told a very incredible story of how they had been obtained from the ancient city of Lximaga, where they were reverenced as gods. A certain Seilor uez, in company with a Canadian and American, penetrated into this ancient city of Central America, where they made the acquaintance of one of the guardian priests of these undersized deities, who was so charmed with the accounts of the outer world, that he resolved to steal the gods of his people, and escape with the strangers. One after the oi the Canadian, the American, and the priest — were overtaken by disaster, and Velasquez alone was left to tell the wondrous tale, with no attestation but such as the children themselves furnished. Professor Owen considered them mere dwarfs, and uthorities held a similar opinion. Belonging probably to some Indian tribe, they were doubtless monstrosities ; and this becoming apparent, interest in them ceased.

azuni.c: AZU'NI, Domenico Alberto, a distinguished jurist, bom at Sassari, in the island of Sardinia, t 3, 1740. He early applied himself to the study of law, devoting himself particularly to the maritime relationships of nations. He became judge of the Tribunal of Commerce at Nizza or Nice ; and in 1795, after that city had been taken by the French, he published a work in which he endeavoured to reduce maritime laws to fixed principles, and which, being recast, was published at Paris in 1S05 under the title of Droit Maritime de V Europe. The work was sufficiently anti-British in tone to secure its author the favourable consideration of Napoleon's ministry, by whom he was appointed one of the commissioners for compiling the new commercial code, the maritime portion being allotted to him. Genoa having been annexed to France, A., in 1807, was appointed president of the Court of Appeal there, where he remained until the fall of Napoleon. Among other things, A. published an Ere Qtographiqwe Politique et Morale de la Sardaigne, and a Dictionary of Mercantile Jurisprudence, and some controversial brochures. For some time after he had withdrawn from Genoa, i ided at Nice, and afterwards in his native island, where he was appointed, by King Charles Felix, judge of the consulate of Cagliari, and librarian to the university of that city. He died in January 1827.

THE second letter in the Hebrew or Phoenician alphabet, and in all alphabets derived from it. belongs to the order of labials, and is of the kind called nuchal or Hat. See Lettei;.s, ALPHABET. Its name in Hebrew is beth, signifying 'house,' probably because its original hieroglyphic or picture form was an outline of a house or tent In the corresponding words of sister-la u . we find b very generally ied by some one of the other labial letters [/>, / (///i), r] ; these substitutions, however, take place not by chance or caprice, but according to l laws. See Philology, CohpABATTVZ, and (Ikimm's Law. The following aresomeex of the interchange of b with other letters: Corresponding to Eng. bear are Sansc. b/iri, Lat. ferre, Gr. pherein: Eng. be, Sansc. bliu, Lat. fio and fax, Gr. pkuo: Eng. "tore, Lat. forare: Eng. o/and off, G r. npo, Lat. ab : Eng. wife, plural wives, Ger. weib, Old H. Ger. wip : Eng. web, weave, theft: Gr. epis- copos, Eng. bishop, Fr. evique. In several . 6 arose out of u (pronounced like r ■ Thus, the original form of bellum, war, was duelltim or dvellum ; of bonus, dvonus ; and the d being dropped (as we drop the sound of /; in knee), the v became hardened into b. Similarly, bis, twice, is for duis. A remarkable interchange sometimes takes place between b and m, as in Sansc. mri, to die ; Lat. mort-, death ; and Gr. brolos, mortal The Greeks pronounced their b (/!) like a v, for they spelled VirgiMut, e.g., BirgUios ; and this continues to be the case in modern Greek. In Latin, during the classical ages at least, the letter was pronounced as it is in English, French, &c. But in the time of the later emperors (beginning with the 3d c. of our era), b was softened down, in the popular i . to a slovenly sound like v; for in inscriptions of this period, such spellings as rrrva for i . are ipiite common. The distinction between the two sounds being once lost sight of, the letter b was frequently substituted for v — as berba for verba, bivus for in'ffti I ftening of b into v in the middle-age Latin, has left braces in the modern Italian and French ; as Lat, habere, Ital avere, Fi.avoir; Lat, tabula, Ital. tarda. A Spaniard, on the contrary, has a tendency to use 6 instead of v; thus he pronounces vivere like bibere, and Jams aa if written Jubis.
